ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of every limited partner, the general partner, all beneficial owners, signatories and counterparties against FINTRAC advisories, the Canadian Sanctions List (Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act schedules), OFAC SDN List, UN Consolidated List, EU and UK HMT consolidated lists, and Interpol notices; enhanced due diligence applies to the Medium_Risk_Enhanced cash-on-delivery e-commerce model, including source-of-wealth documentation for non-resident contributors, real-time transaction monitoring on Airwallex and local logistics remittance rails, and annual KYC refresh plus threshold-triggered re-verification.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_disclosure_level_notes: Alberta's Beneficial Ownership Transparency Act register is filed with the Registrar and is accessible to law enforcement, tax authorities and prescribed regulators; it is not a fully public register, and nominee arrangements remain permissible only where the controlling natural persons are disclosed at the 25% threshold.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta) filed through authorized Corporate Registry service providers using the Corporate Registry Search System (CORES) and the NUANS name search network; official reference portal: alberta.ca/corporate-registry
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Registry working language is English; French and bilingual names are accepted where transliterated into Latin script; non-Latin investor names must be fully transliterated into Latin script on all filings; the limited partnership name must conclude with 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.', 'LP', 'société en commandite' or 'S.E.C.' as a mandatory legal element; punctuation and permitted characters follow the Business Names Act General Regulation.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: An Alberta name reservation is valid for 90 days and cannot be extended; upon expiry a fresh NUANS search and new reservation application must be filed. On rejection for lack of distinctiveness: obtain written consent from the holder of the conflicting name and resubmit, or add a distinctive geographic or descriptive element. On rejection for a prohibited or sensitive token: obtain prior written approval from the supervising Alberta minister or regulator (e.g., approval under the Financial Institutions and Credit Unions Act for bank, trust, insurance or loan words) and attach the approval to the resubmission. Administrative remedy: submit a written reconsideration request to the Registrar of Companies (Service Alberta) within 30 days of refusal citing the distinguishing elements; a final refusal may be challenged by judicial review before the Court of King's Bench of Alberta under the Alberta Rules of Court. Parallel LP-specific remedy: register under an alternative permitted name and, where the preferred name is only marginally similar, apply to register a distinguishing extra element with the Registrar.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for a mail-order e-commerce LP with no storefront: a street address in Alberta (a post office box alone is prohibited) with a registered agent or mail-forwarding arrangement satisfies the statutory registered office requirement, provided documents can be physically served at that address during normal business hours and the beneficial ownership register remains accessible at the registered office or another Alberta location designated by the general partner.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low quantified estimate of 5-10%: the Alberta registry does not routinely conduct unannounced physical inspections of limited partnerships lacking a fixed commercial premise; on-site inspection risk is triggered mainly by FINTRAC or RCMP AML investigations, CRA tax audit verification visits, or repeated service-of-process failures at the registered office.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Alberta Limited Partnership Act (R.S.A. 2000, c. L-4) and Partnership Act (R.S.A. 2000, c. P-3), sections 2-10 on formation, registration and limited liability
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Certificate of Limited Partnership (Form 1 - Declaration of Limited Partnership)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital requirement under Alberta law; capital contributions are at the discretion of partners and may be made in cash or property
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that the General Partner of the proposed Limited Partnership subscribes for the initial capital contribution of ten thousand Canadian dollars (CAD 10,000); FURTHER RESOLVED that the registered office of the Limited Partnership shall be established at the address provided in the Declaration of Limited Partnership; FURTHER RESOLVED that [General Partner Full Legal Name] is appointed as the sole General Partner with full authority to manage the business affairs of the Limited Partnership, including the execution of all contracts, opening of bank accounts, and filing of all statutory documents with the Alberta Corporate Registry; FURTHER RESOLVED that the General Partner shall maintain accurate books and records in accordance with the Partnership Act and Limited Partnership Act; FURTHER RESOLVED that the General Partner shall ensure compliance with all applicable federal and provincial laws, including but not limited to the Income Tax Act and any applicable anti-money laundering regulations; FURTHER RESOLVED that this resolution shall remain in effect until revoked by a majority of the General Partner or as otherwise provided in the partnership agreement.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), including the Business Registration Online portal and My Business Account portal. Alberta corporate and partnership registrations are administered separately by Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction through the Alberta Corporate Registry.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: 1. Complete formation or registration of the Alberta limited partnership with the Alberta Corporate Registry and obtain the partnership registration evidence. 2. Apply to the CRA for a nine-digit Business Number (BN) using Business Registration Online, the CRA telephone service, or the prescribed registration process for non-residents. A Canadian limited partnership generally requires a BN where it has Canadian tax filing or program-account obligations. 3. Open the applicable CRA program accounts: GST/HST account (RT) when registration is required or voluntarily elected; Information Returns account (RZ) where applicable; and any other account required by the partnership's activities. 4. Register for a T5013 partnership information return account where the statutory filing conditions apply, including applicable partnership size, income, or partner-status conditions. 5. Provide legal formation documents, Canadian business address or authorized representative details, responsible-person information, ownership and control information, business activity descriptions, fiscal-period information, and identity-verification documents. 6. A non-resident entity must provide evidence of its legal existence, authority to carry on the relevant Canadian activities, Canadian commercial nexus, and an authorized Canadian contact where requested. 7. The GST/HST account does not replace the BN: the standard identifier is the BN followed by the applicable CRA program suffix, including RT for GST/HST. Canada does not generally issue a separate universal entity TIN equivalent to a single-purpose foreign TIN; the BN and relevant program-account number perform the principal tax-identification functions.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no general United States-style check-the-box election for a Canadian limited partnership. A valid limited partnership is generally taxed as a partnership for Canadian income-tax purposes, with income, losses, and other fiscal amounts determined at the partnership level and allocated to partners under the Income Tax Act and the partnership agreement, subject to statutory allocation rules. Available mechanisms may include a section 96 partnership computation, a section 97(2) rollover for qualifying transfers of property to a Canadian partnership, and partnership agreement elections or designations where expressly authorized by statute. A partnership cannot generally elect to be treated as a Canadian corporation solely by filing a classification form. Foreign classification elections, including a U.S. check-the-box election, do not automatically control Canadian classification and may create cross-border hybrid-entity or hybrid-mismatch issues. Canadian anti-hybrid mismatch rules must be reviewed where foreign deductions, inclusions, or entity classifications produce a deduction/non-inclusion or duplicate-deduction outcome.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST), with Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) applying in participating provinces. Alberta does not impose a general provincial sales tax; Alberta taxable supplies are generally subject to federal GST only.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 of worldwide taxable supplies, including zero-rated supplies and subject to the statutory small-supplier aggregation rules, measured over a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters. The threshold does not apply in the same manner to every category of supplier, and specific rules apply to non-resident digital-economy suppliers, taxi or ride-sharing operators, charities, public institutions, and persons making only exempt supplies. A supplier may voluntarily register below the threshold if it carries on commercial activities and satisfies the registration requirements.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no general federal real-time GST invoice-clearance, mandatory electronic-invoicing, or continuous transaction-control regime for ordinary Alberta businesses. Registered suppliers must issue GST/HST invoices or other prescribed supporting documentation containing sufficient information to substantiate the consideration, GST/HST rate, tax amount, supplier identity, registration number where required, and applicable documentary details. Electronic invoices and electronic business records are generally acceptable if they preserve integrity, accessibility, readability, and auditability. CRA records must generally be retained for six years from the end of the relevant year, subject to longer periods or unresolved-objection and appeal rules. Certain public-sector procurement arrangements may impose separate electronic-invoicing specifications, but they do not constitute a universal tax-clearance mandate. Customs export reporting is separate from GST invoicing and may require electronic filing through the Canada Border Services Agency's Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS).

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods exported from Canada are generally zero-rated at 0% GST when they are supplied in Canada and exported in accordance with the Exported Goods provisions of the Excise Tax Act, including delivery or shipment to a destination outside Canada and retention of evidence establishing export. For an Alberta cash-on-delivery e-commerce business, the supplier should retain the customer order, sales invoice, payment or collection record, carrier and fulfillment records, shipping address, tracking data, proof of delivery outside Canada, customs documentation where applicable, and evidence that the goods were not consumed, used, or supplied in Canada before export. Goods removed from Canada by a non-resident purchaser may qualify only where the statutory conditions and documentation requirements are met; merely stating a foreign delivery address is insufficient. Services supplied to non-residents may be zero-rated only where a specific Excise Tax Act provision applies. The general exported-services rules are subject to exclusions and conditions, including services relating to real property situated in Canada, tangible personal property situated in Canada, services performed in respect of persons physically present in Canada, and other expressly excluded services. Export zero-rating does not eliminate customs duties, import GST, foreign import VAT, or destination-country tax obligations.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Border Services Agency export declaration through the Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS), where required by the Customs Act and applicable export-reporting rules; commercial exports to the United States are subject to distinct reporting exceptions and controlled-goods rules.
Commercial invoice or equivalent electronic sales documentation identifying the exporter, purchaser or consignee, description, quantity, value, currency, origin, destination, and terms of sale.
Bill of lading, air waybill, courier manifest, postal record, or equivalent carrier document.
Proof of shipment and delivery outside Canada, including carrier tracking, delivery confirmation, warehouse release records, and fulfillment records.
Customer order, payment or cash-on-delivery settlement record, and records linking the order to the exported goods.
Import or customs-entry documentation in the destination country where available and relevant to the transaction.
Proof of export and GST accounting records sufficient to substantiate the zero-rated treatment during a CRA audit.

Inward remittance certificate: not generally a Canadian statutory requirement for GST zero-rating or ordinary export substantiation. Foreign-exchange evidence may nevertheless be retained where required by a financial institution, payment intermediary, financing arrangement, or destination-country law.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Canada generally imposes no universal statutory requirement to repatriate export proceeds within 180 days. A GST registrant must maintain reliable books and records and prove that each zero-rated supply satisfies the Excise Tax Act. CRA may reassess the supplier for GST that should have been charged, deny input tax credits or GST/HST rebates, impose arrears interest, and apply penalties for late filing, failure to remit, false statements, gross negligence, or repeated non-compliance. The gross-negligence penalty can generally be 50% of the understated tax or improperly claimed amount, subject to the statutory rules. False statements, obstruction, destruction of records, or deliberate tax evasion may result in additional civil penalties or criminal prosecution, including fines and imprisonment. Incorrect customs declarations may trigger Canada Border Services Agency administrative monetary penalties, reassessment of duties and taxes, seizure or forfeiture consequences, and other enforcement measures. A zero-rating error is normally reassessed for the applicable statutory assessment period, subject to the ordinary limitation rules and extended or unlimited periods applicable to misrepresentation, fraud, or failure to file or keep required records.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), with prudential supervision by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), AML/ATF transaction monitoring and wire-reporting enforcement by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), and residual trade/sanctions enforcement by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and Global Affairs Canada. Exchange control policy is exercised by the Minister of Finance under the Currency Act and the Bank of Canada Act; Canada maintains no separate foreign-exchange licensing authority.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada operates a fully liberalized capital and current account regime. The Canadian dollar is freely convertible for residents and non-residents at market rates. No central bank approval is required for profit remittance, partnership distributions, or repatriation of capital, provided the transactions are not connected to sanctioned jurisdictions under the Special Economic Measures Act or the United Nations Act. For a Canadian limited partnership, distributions to non-resident partners are generally subject to Part XIII Canadian withholding tax (normally 25% unless reduced by an income tax treaty), but this is a tax compliance matter rather than a currency control or convertibility hurdle. For proving treaty entitlement, the non-resident partner must provide a valid Canada Revenue Agency form NR301, NR302, or NR303, as applicable. Mail-order retail operations with cash-on-delivery settlement carry no additional currency convertibility restriction.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada does not impose any mandatory surrender, repatriation timeline, or conversion ratio for export proceeds. Foreign currency export receipts may be retained in offshore accounts or sold on the interbank market freely. However, financial institutions must report cross-border electronic funds transfers of C$10,000 or more to FINTRAC within 24 hours, and any transaction physically transporting currency or monetary instruments over C$10,000 must be reported to the CBSA under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act. Customs export declarations are required for controlled or regulated goods, but no exchange-control surrender requirement exists.

Operating Account and USD clearing sub-account; escrow desk for subscription-in-kind
Operating Account with strong correspondent network in emerging Latin American and Asian corridors; Capital Escrow Account available

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating for offshore digital electronic money institutions (EMIs) is Medium-High, but subject to strict legal constraints. Offshore EMIs (e.g., Airwallex, Windward, Currencycloud) may operate safely as payment initiation or collection service providers only when they are registered as Money Services Businesses (MSBs) with FINTRAC and, where applicable, comply with the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) once fully in force. A pure offshore EMI holding client funds in Canada without a Canadian bank partner and without FINTRAC registration is not legal. The trio of Airwallex, local logistics remittance providers, and a Canadian bank is permissible when the EMI merely facilitates collection through the bank's payment gateway and the LP is designated as the merchant of record. The legal contract must ensure that all cash-on-delivery funds are reconciled daily, subject to AML sanctions screening, and remitted to the LP's bank account via the EMI's Canadian bank settlement account. No statutory license is required for the LP itself, because ISIC 4791 mail-order retail is not a regulated financial activity; however any payment intermediary used must be appropriately licensed.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical presence in Canada is required by all major Tier-1 banks for a newly formed Alberta Limited Partnership with a non-resident general partner or multiple offshore limited partners. The initial KYC interview must be conducted with the General Partner or a designated senior officer; Canadian banks permit remote video verification for the individual, but legal entity documentation must be certified by a Canadian legal counsel or notary. In practice, all directors/partners owning 25% or more of the LP must provide certified passports, proof of residential address, source of funds, and source of wealth. Several banks will insist on an in-person visit of the General Partner if the emerging market jurisdiction is considered higher risk or if the LP cannot demonstrate a local physical premises and operating substance. A clean alternative is to appoint a Canadian resident General Partner and a Canadian registered agent; remote account opening then becomes feasible, usually within 10–15 business days.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership opacity of the limited partnership, particularly multiple limited partners in emerging market code COD jurisdictions
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide an entity ownership and control chain chart registered with Alberta Corporate Registry under the Business Corporations Act / Partnership Act; executed LP agreement listing all partners and percentage interests; certified passports and proof of residential address for every partner holding 25% or more; source of wealth summary, bank references, and a legal opinion from Canadian counsel confirming the LP is validly constituted.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-risk geographic exposure combined with cash-on-delivery e-commerce settlement, which can attract enhanced AML underwriting
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Present an up-to-date sanctions screening report for all partners against Canadian consolidated sanctions lists; evidence of a genuine Canadian business footprint (office lease, payroll records, Alberta provincial tax registration and CRA business number); a written business plan and projected settlement volume split between Canadian and foreign logistics partners; and a detailed transaction-flow diagram showing the logistics remittance provider's licensing status.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of third-party logistics remittance and cash collection, creating an unregulated cash-in-network that may be flagged as structurally risky
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide executed service agreements with the logistics provider and payment processor, explicitly identifying the LP as merchant of record; ensure the processors are licensed MSBs or Exempt Payment Facilitators; deliver monthly transactional reconciliation reports and audit trail exports; arrange for the bank to conduct a limited pre-approval of the processor; and supply a processor compliance certificate showing no sanctions overlaps.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large inbound capital injection from an unrelated third-party or a tax-haven intermediary on behalf of a limited partner, triggering unexplained wealth orders or FINTRAC wire reports
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide the capital call notice, contribution agreement, and LP resolution approving the injection; bank statement of the originator showing a clear source of funds; a notarized statutory declaration of the funder identifying the commercial rationale; and an opinion from counsel confirming the funds are sourced from legitimate operations and not from any listed sanctions target.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital contributions to the Alberta LP should be routed as a SWIFT MT103 corporate treasury payment. The bank instruction must use the LP's full legal name and Alberta corporate registry number (e.g., 'ABC CA LP / ARN 123456789'); the remitter should use Field 50K with full source account; the beneficiary in Field 59 must be the LP's own operating or capital escrow account. In Field 70 or a designated purpose code, include a clear description: 'LPK-2025-AB-001 capital contribution – ABC CA LP' and a correlation to the capital call notice. For cross-border wires over C$10,000, the sending financial institution must report the transfer to FINTRAC automatically; no separate filing by the LP is required, but the LP should retain the contribution agreement, capital call, and bank confirmation for audit. All inbound injections must be reconciled against the partner's capital ledger and, for non-resident partners, subjected to treaty entitlement review before distribution. For structuring, two-tranche routing is preferred: first a smaller validation transfer (C$5,000 or equivalent) to confirm banking details, then the full contribution via a cleared, pre-verified wire. Avoid any use of crypto or cross-border cash-courier transfers.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Trade settlements for inventory, logistics, and COD remittances should be cleared through SWIFT MT103 for immediate cross-border supplier payments, using the purpose code 'Goods Purchase' or 'Commercial Trade Settlement' and referencing the invoice and purchase order number. For high-value or bulk purchases from emerging markets, an irrevocable, at-sight Commercial Letter of Credit (MT700) is permissible and recommended to reduce counterparty risk; the LC must incorporate a clean Incoterms 2020 rule (e.g., FOB/EXW) and require documents to conform exactly to the commercial invoice and CBSA import declaration. Domestic cash-on-delivery logistics remittances may be consolidated through an automated clearing house (ACH) or Interac e-Transfer for small values, but for larger aggregate amounts, use a LVTS (Large Value Transfer System) wire via the Tier-1 bank. For country-specific disallowed payment rails, every outbound transfer must be screened against Global Affairs Canada and OSFI sanctioned jurisdictions before execution. All outbound disbursements should be supported by a signed payment instruction, invoice, logistics proforma, and a treasury-approved FX rate record when payment is denominated in a foreign currency.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Over-the-counter (OTC) outright FX forwards for CAD/USD and CAD/EUR up to 12 months, executed under a bank ISDA 2002 or Canadian Master Forward Agreement

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for restricted or illiquid emerging-market currencies where the local currency is not fully deliverable (e.g., USD/CNH, USD/BRL, USD/INR), subject to bank counterparty credit limits and Canada laundering checks
Cross-currency swaps (CCS) matching the commercial working-capital cycle, enabling exchange of principal and floating/ fixed interest in CAD against emerging-market or USD proceeds
Plain-vanilla FX swaps (swap of principal and interest at spot with a simultaneous offsetting forward) for temporary currency surplus recycling

Cancellable FX forward contracts (target redemption forwards) offered by Canadian banks for hedging expected monthly USD revenue from cross-border sales; only when clearly reducing commercial exchange risk
Vanilla call options or put options on FX for the LP's trade receipts; executed with an options clearing broker or a major Canadian bank under the local over-the-counter derivatives regime

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary date of the limited partnership's registration
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of CAD 60; continued non-filing for two consecutive anniversaries triggers administrative dissolution strike-off by the Registrar.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For Canadian-resident partners: March 31 following the calendar year end of the fiscal period; for partnerships with any non-resident partner: June 15 following the calendar year end.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: CRA penalty of CAD 50 per partner per month for late filing, minimum CAD 100, maximum CAD 2,500; partners may lose loss deductibility for 12 months if non-filing persists.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Alberta Corporate Tax (Partnership Allocation) Information Confirmation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Treasury Board and Finance / CRA
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No standalone Alberta LP filing; allocation is included in each partner's Alberta corporate/personal tax return by the partner's filing deadline (June 15 for individuals, two months after corporate year-end).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Partner-level late-filing penalties apply: 5% of balance owing plus 1% per month; repeated non-compliance may trigger re-assessment and interest charges.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit is required for Alberta limited partnerships under the Partnership Act; audits arise only if required by the partnership agreement, an investing regulator, or a financial institution lending covenant.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS or ASPE per partnership agreement; if no audit is required, annual financial statements may be prepared on a tax-basis for Canadian partnership tax allocations and partner capital statement maintenance.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta LPs have no statutory annual UBO filing obligation to the provincial registry. Partner identity/ownership percentages are maintained in the Register of Partners and updated upon any transfer or admission. General partners, if corporations, must maintain a separately filed significant-individual register under the Alberta Business Corporations Act. FINTRAC reporting entities will collect ownership confirmation for payments above CAD 10,000.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Partners (currently admitted limited and general partners, contribution amounts, profit-sharing percentages)
Register of General Partner (including, if corporate general partner, its directors and registered office)
Minute Book (partnership consents, amendments to the limited partnership agreement, annual meeting resolutions if applicable)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: N/A (no statutory audit); if required by contract, small-LP certified review and audit ranges USD 5,000 - 15,000

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 0% at the Alberta Limited Partnership (CA_LP) level: the LP is fiscally transparent and files only the T5013 information return; corporate partners are taxed at the combined federal + Alberta general rate of 23% (15% federal + 8% Alberta) on their allocable share of Canadian-source partnership income.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) partners may claim the federal small business deduction (federal 9% + Alberta 2% = 11% combined on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income allocated from the LP); accelerated capital cost allowance (Class 50 for computers/software at 55% declining balance, Class 44 for patents and software, Class 10.1 for delivery vehicles); immediate expensing of up to CAD 1.5 million of eligible capital property for CCPCs; scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) refundable investment tax credits for e-commerce software and COD logistics innovation.
